title: Registering at a parish
summary: In the United States most parishes keep a list of registered households. Church law already makes you a member of the parish where you live (your territorial parish), but registering is how a US parish actually knows you. Registration is usually the first thing a parish asks about when you request a sacrament or a sponsor letter. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Register as soon as you move or start attending. Some parishes want you registered and active for a few months before they will issue a sponsor letter or schedule a wedding or baptism. Ask what their waiting period is.
contact: The parish office (many parishes also have an online registration form on their website)

documents.name: Registration form
documents.detail: The parish's own form, on paper or online. It asks for names, address, phone, email and the sacraments each household member has received.

documents.name: Home address and contact information
documents.detail: Your territorial parish is decided by where you live. Some parishes also register people from outside their boundaries.

documents.name: Dates of birth for each household member
documents.detail: Used for religious education placement and for the parish's records

documents.name: Sacraments received, with the parish of each
documents.detail: Baptism, First Communion, Confirmation and Marriage, with the name and city of the parish where each took place. You don't need certificates to register, but have these details ready.
documents.where: You or your family. If unsure, the parish of baptism can confirm

documents.name: Marriage information
documents.detail: Date and place of marriage, and whether it was in the Catholic Church. Also note any prior marriages or annulments, if relevant.

documents.name: Children's information
documents.detail: Names, dates of birth, schools and grades, and the sacraments each child has received

documents.name: Photo ID
documents.detail: Rarely needed for registration itself, but sometimes asked for when you pick up sponsor letters or certificates
documents.where: Your state ID or driver's license

steps: Find your territorial parish. Use your diocese's online parish finder or call the diocesan office with your address. You can choose to register at a different parish if it will accept you.
Fill out the registration form, online or at the parish office
List every household member and the sacraments each has received
Optional: sign up for offertory envelopes or online giving. Some parishes treat regular use of envelopes as evidence that you are an 'active' parishioner, and that can matter for sponsor letters.
Keep the confirmation email or welcome letter, and tell the office when you move or your household changes
dayOf: There is no ceremony. Some parishes hold a 'new parishioner' welcome event or Mass several times a year.

faq.q: Do I have to register to be Catholic or go to Mass?
faq.a: No. Anyone may attend Mass anywhere, and Church law makes you a member of your territorial parish by where you live. Registration is a US administrative practice. Parishes rely on it heavily, though, especially for sponsor letters, sacramental preparation, Catholic school tuition rates and weddings.

faq.q: Why does my parish say I'm not 'active' enough for a sponsor letter?
faq.a: Many parishes will only vouch for people they know. They may ask that you have been registered for a few months and attend regularly. Talk to the pastor directly. He can often vouch for you if he knows you.

faq.q: Can I register at a parish outside my neighborhood?
faq.a: Usually yes. Many US dioceses let you register at any parish that will accept you. Ask the parish.

title: Getting your sacramental records (baptismal certificate 'with notations')
summary: Your official Catholic record lives in the baptismal register of the parish where you were baptized. Confirmation, marriage, ordination, religious profession and declarations of nullity are noted in the margin of that entry (Can. 535 §2). A certificate 'with notations' is a fresh copy of that entry, including the notes. You'll need one for marriage, ordination and religious life, and often for Confirmation, OCIA, or serving as a godparent. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Request it early. Many parishes answer within 1–3 weeks, but closed or merged parishes, overseas parishes and archives can take much longer. For a wedding, most US parishes want a certificate issued within the last 6 months, so time the request to fall inside that window.
contact: The parish office of the parish where you were baptized. If that parish has closed or merged, contact its successor parish or the diocesan archives or chancery.

documents.name: Written or online request
documents.detail: Many parishes take requests by phone, email or an online form. Some want a signed written request. State what the certificate is for (e.g. 'for marriage'), because that tells them to include notations and to issue a newly dated copy.

documents.name: Your full name at baptism
documents.detail: Give the name exactly as it would have been recorded, including your birth surname if it has changed since

documents.name: Date and place of birth
documents.detail: Used to locate the entry

documents.name: Approximate date of baptism
documents.detail: The year is usually enough

documents.name: Parents' full names, including mother's maiden name
documents.detail: Baptismal registers are indexed this way

documents.name: Photo ID
documents.detail: Some parishes require ID before releasing a record, especially if you pick it up in person
documents.where: Your state ID or driver's license

documents.name: Return address or the receiving parish's address
documents.detail: For marriage and other official uses, many parishes send the certificate straight to the requesting parish or tribunal. They may refuse to give it to you, or require that the envelope stay sealed.

documents.name: Proof of name change or adoption
documents.detail: Only if your current name doesn't match the register. Records of adopted persons are handled confidentially, so expect extra steps.

documents.name: Offering
documents.detail: Some parishes ask for a small offering to cover processing or postage. Ask the parish. Many charge nothing.

steps: Find out where you were baptized: parish name, city, and approximate year. Family members, baptismal candles and gowns, and photos often help.
Look up the parish online. If it has closed or merged, call the diocese's chancery or archives and ask which parish now holds its registers.
Contact the parish office and ask for a 'baptismal certificate with notations, newly issued' for your stated purpose
Give the identifying details listed in the documents section
Say where it should go: to you, or directly to the parish or tribunal that needs it
Check the certificate when it arrives: names, dates, and any confirmation or marriage notations
If you were baptized on a US military installation, contact the Archdiocese for the Military Services, which holds those registers
If you were baptized outside the US, write to that parish or its diocese. Allow extra time, and ask whether a translation will be needed.
dayOf: There is no ceremony. Check that the certificate carries the parish seal and a recent issue date if it is for marriage.

faq.q: Why can't I just use the certificate my parents got at my baptism?
faq.a: That souvenir certificate records only the baptism itself. A newly issued copy shows the current notations (confirmation, marriage, and so on), which is how the Church verifies, for example, that you are free to marry.

faq.q: Why must it be issued within 6 months for a wedding?
faq.a: This is common US diocesan practice, not a universal canon. A recent copy shows that no marriage has been noted since it was issued. Some dioceses use a different window, so ask your parish.

faq.q: I can't find any record of my baptism. What now?
faq.a: Tell your pastor. Baptism can sometimes be proved by the sworn statement of a witness (for example, a godparent or a parent who was present). If baptism genuinely can't be established, the pastor will explain the options, which may include conditional baptism.

faq.q: Where is my Confirmation recorded?
faq.a: In the confirmation register of the parish where you were confirmed. That parish should also notify your parish of baptism, which notes it in your baptismal record. If the notation is missing, the confirming parish can issue a confirmation certificate.

title: Baptism (infants & young children)
summary: Baptism is the first sacrament. It frees from sin, makes the child a member of Christ and the Church, and opens the way to the other sacraments. Catholic parents are obliged to have their infants baptized within the first few weeks after birth (Can. 867 §1). Children who have reached the age of reason, usually about 7, follow the children's OCIA path instead. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Contact the parish during pregnancy or soon after birth. Allow about 1–3 months to complete the class and paperwork and get a date. Many parishes baptize on set Sundays each month.
contact: The parish office of your parish. Some parishes have a baptism coordinator. Your parish will generally baptize the child (Can. 857 §2). If you want the baptism at another parish, you usually need permission from your own pastor.

documents.name: Child's birth certificate
documents.detail: Copy of the civil birth certificate. The parish uses it to record names, date and place of birth, and parents' names exactly.
documents.where: State or county vital records office (hospital paperwork is usually not enough)

documents.name: Parish baptism registration form
documents.detail: The parish's form with the child's and parents' details and the chosen name(s), plus the godparent(s)' names and parishes

documents.name: Proof of parents' parish registration
documents.detail: Most parishes baptize children of registered, practicing families, or ask why you are coming to them

documents.name: Godparent sponsor certificate(s) / letter(s) of eligibility
documents.detail: One for each godparent who is not registered at the baptizing parish. Each godparent gets theirs from their own parish, and it certifies they meet Can. 874. Many parishes want it signed within the last 6 months.

documents.name: Christian witness information
documents.detail: If a baptized non-Catholic serves as a Christian witness, the parish may ask for their name and church, and sometimes proof of baptism

documents.name: Certificate of completion of the parents' baptism class
documents.detail: Needed if you took the class at a different parish
documents.where: Parish where you took the class

documents.name: Parents' marriage information
documents.detail: Some parishes ask whether, where and when the parents married. Parents' marital status is not a bar to a child's baptism, but the pastor may use it as a pastoral opening.

documents.name: Letter of permission from your own pastor
documents.detail: Only if the baptism takes place outside your own parish

requirements: Chosen by the person being baptized, the parents, or (failing them) the pastor, and willing to take on the role (Can. 874 §1, 1°)
At least 16 years old, unless the diocesan bishop has set a different age or the pastor grants an exception for a just cause (Can. 874 §1, 2°)
A Catholic who has been confirmed and has received the Most Holy Eucharist (Can. 874 §1, 3°)
Leads a life of faith in keeping with the role (Can. 874 §1, 3°); in US practice this is usually read as attending Mass regularly and, if married, being in a marriage recognized by the Church
Not under a canonical penalty legitimately imposed or declared (Can. 874 §1, 4°)
Not the father or mother of the person being baptized (Can. 874 §1, 5°)
Only one godparent is required; if there are two, they must be one male and one female (Can. 873)
documents: Sponsor certificate / letter of eligibility from the godparent's own parish
Some parishes also require the godparent to attend the baptism class

requirements: A baptized Christian of another church or community, admitted only together with a Catholic godparent (Can. 874 §2)
Is recorded as a witness, not as a godparent
documents: Sometimes proof of baptism. Ask the parish.

requirements: At least one parent (or the person legally in their place) consents to the baptism (Can. 868 §1, 1°)

There must be a founded hope that the child will be brought up in the Catholic faith. If that hope is altogether lacking, the baptism is delayed, not refused, and the pastor explains why (Can. 868 §1, 2°).

steps: Register at your parish if you haven't
Call the parish office during pregnancy or right after birth, and ask about class dates and baptism dates
Choose godparent(s) and ask each to request a sponsor certificate from their own parish
Order a copy of the birth certificate as soon as the state issues it
Attend the parents' baptism preparation session (godparents are often invited or required)
Turn in the registration form, birth certificate, and sponsor certificates by the parish deadline
Confirm the date, time, and any rehearsal, and ask about photography rules
After the baptism, keep the certificate you're given. The official record stays in the parish register for life.
classes: A baptism preparation class for parents, often a single session of 1–3 hours. Some parishes waive it for second and later children if taken recently. Godparents are often encouraged or required to attend. Some dioceses add a home visit or a second session.
dayOf: Arrive early. The celebrant may meet you at the door or in the narthex.
Bring a white garment for the child (or one is provided), and possibly a baptismal candle. Many parishes provide the candle. Ask.

Godparents and parents stand with the child. The rite includes the welcome and naming, readings, the prayer of exorcism and anointing with the oil of catechumens, renunciation of sin and profession of faith, the baptism (immersion or pouring of water), anointing with chrism, the white garment, the lighted candle, and the Lord's Prayer and blessing.
Baptisms may take place during Sunday Mass or in a separate ceremony, often Sunday afternoon
A stipend/offering is customary; ask the parish. Never assume a fixed fee.
Sign or verify the register entry if asked, and collect the baptismal certificate

faq.q: Can a non-Catholic be a godparent?
faq.a: A baptized non-Catholic Christian may serve as a 'Christian witness' alongside a Catholic godparent, but not as the godparent (Can. 874 §2). Someone who is not baptized cannot serve in either role.

faq.q: Do we need two godparents?
faq.a: No. One godparent is enough. If you have two, they must be one man and one woman (Can. 873).

faq.q: What if the baby is in danger of death?
faq.a: Baptize without delay (Can. 867 §2). Call the hospital chaplain or a priest. In an emergency anyone, even a non-Catholic, can baptize by pouring water on the head while saying 'N., I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,' intending to do what the Church does (Can. 861 §2). Afterward, tell the parish so it can be recorded.

faq.q: Our parents' marriage isn't recognized by the Church. Can our child still be baptized?
faq.a: Generally yes. The child's baptism isn't conditioned on the parents' marital status. The pastor needs a founded hope that the child will be raised Catholic, and he may invite you to talk about convalidation.

faq.q: Can a godparent participate by proxy?
faq.a: Many US parishes allow a proxy to stand in for a godparent who can't travel. The absent godparent is recorded, but must still meet the requirements and provide a sponsor certificate. Ask your parish.

faq.q: Does the child need a saint's name?
faq.a: No. Church law asks only that the name not be foreign to Christian sensibility (Can. 855).

title: Baptism (adults and children over about 7)
summary: Unbaptized adults, and children who have reached the age of reason (about 7), are prepared through the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults (OCIA). They receive Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion together, normally at the Easter Vigil. See the OCIA entry for the full process and paperwork. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Contact the parish any time of year. Many parishes run inquiry sessions year-round. Formation commonly lasts at least a year, and the sacraments are usually celebrated at the Easter Vigil.
contact: Your parish's OCIA coordinator (formerly called RCIA) or the parish office

documents.name: See the OCIA entry
documents.detail: The complete checklist (birth certificate, marriage history, sponsor letter, etc.) is in the OCIA entry

documents.name: Birth certificate
documents.detail: Used to record your legal name and date and place of birth
documents.where: State or county vital records office

documents.name: Marriage history
documents.detail: If you are married or have been married before, this must be reviewed, and any previous marriages resolved, before you receive the sacraments
documents.where: You. Copies of marriage, divorce and death certificates

requirements: Chosen by the person being baptized, the parents, or (failing them) the pastor, and willing to take on the role (Can. 874 §1, 1°)
At least 16 years old, unless the diocesan bishop has set a different age or the pastor grants an exception for a just cause (Can. 874 §1, 2°)
A Catholic who has been confirmed and has received the Most Holy Eucharist (Can. 874 §1, 3°)
Leads a life of faith in keeping with the role (Can. 874 §1, 3°); in US practice this is usually read as attending Mass regularly and, if married, being in a marriage recognized by the Church
Not under a canonical penalty legitimately imposed or declared (Can. 874 §1, 4°)
Not the father or mother of the person being baptized (Can. 874 §1, 5°)
Only one godparent is required; if there are two, they must be one male and one female (Can. 873)
documents: Sponsor certificate from the sponsor's own parish, unless they are a parishioner where you are being baptized

steps: Contact the parish OCIA coordinator
Attend inquiry sessions with no commitment
Follow the OCIA stages described in the OCIA entry
dayOf: Usually the Easter Vigil: Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion in one celebration

faq.q: Why can't my 9-year-old just be baptized like a baby?
faq.a: Church law treats anyone who has reached the use of reason as an adult for baptism (Can. 852 §1). The child is prepared through the children's adaptation of OCIA, and normally receives all three sacraments of initiation together.

faq.q: I was baptized in another Christian church. Do I need to be baptized again?
faq.a: No. A valid baptism in another Christian church is never repeated. Conditional baptism happens only if there is serious doubt about validity (Can. 869). You would be received into full communion instead (see OCIA).

sources: Order of Christian Initiation of Adults

title: First Reconciliation (First Confession)
summary: In the Sacrament of Penance, a baptized person confesses sins to a priest and receives absolution. Catholic children make their first confession before their First Communion (Can. 914). In the US this is usually in 2nd grade, around age 7. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Enroll the child in the parish religious education program (or Catholic school sacramental program) by the start of the school year. First Reconciliation is usually celebrated in the fall to winter or Lent of the preparation year.
contact: The parish Director of Religious Education (DRE) or faith formation office, or the Catholic school if the child attends one

documents.name: Child's baptismal certificate
documents.detail: Needed if the child was baptized at another parish. It confirms the child is baptized Catholic and gives the record's location.

documents.name: Religious education registration form
documents.detail: Enrollment in the parish program or Catholic school sacrament program

documents.name: Proof of prior year of religious education
documents.detail: Many US dioceses require two consecutive years of formation: the year before plus the sacrament year. Transfer students may need records from their previous program.
documents.where: Previous parish program or Catholic school

documents.name: Program fee or registration payment
documents.detail: Some religious education programs charge a registration fee to cover materials. Amounts vary, and assistance is usually available. Ask the parish.

documents.name: Parish registration
documents.detail: Many programs require the family to be registered

requirements: Parents are the first teachers of the faith. Most programs require parents to attend one or more preparation meetings.
Help the child prepare at home (examination of conscience, Act of Contrition)

steps: Register the family at the parish if you haven't
Enroll the child in religious education or the Catholic school sacrament program, usually for 1st and 2nd grade
Submit the baptismal certificate if the child was baptized elsewhere
Attend parent meetings and complete any at-home lessons
Help the child learn an Act of Contrition and how confession works. Many parishes give children a card to bring.
Attend the scheduled First Reconciliation service
classes: Usually part of a 2-year preparation (1st and 2nd grade) through the parish program or Catholic school, plus parent meetings. Older children who missed it are often placed in an age-appropriate catch-up or 'sacrament prep' class.
dayOf: Usually a parish penance service: opening prayer, Scripture, examination of conscience, then each child goes individually to a priest
The child may confess face-to-face or behind a screen, according to parish and diocesan custom
Bring the Act of Contrition card if the parish gave one
No special clothing is required. Ordinary 'church clothes' are typical.
Some parishes have a small celebration afterward

faq.q: Does my child need a sponsor for First Reconciliation?
faq.a: No. Sponsors are for Baptism and Confirmation.

faq.q: Is what my child says kept secret?
faq.a: Yes. The seal of confession is absolute. A priest may never reveal what is confessed (Can. 983).

faq.q: My child is older and never made a first confession. Is it too late?
faq.a: No. Contact the DRE. Older children are placed in an age-appropriate preparation program.

title: First Holy Communion
summary: In the Eucharist, Catholics receive the Body and Blood of Christ. A baptized Catholic child receives First Communion once he or she has reached the use of reason, has sufficient knowledge and careful preparation, and has first made a sacramental confession (Can. 913–914). In the US this is usually in 2nd grade, often in the spring. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Enroll in parish religious education or the Catholic school program by the start of the school year. Most US dioceses expect two consecutive years of formation. First Communion Masses are usually held in April or May.
contact: The parish Director of Religious Education (DRE) or faith formation office, or the Catholic school

documents.name: Child's baptismal certificate
documents.detail: Needed if the child was baptized at another parish. Many parishes ask for it even for their own parishioners so the record is on file.

documents.name: Proof of First Reconciliation
documents.detail: First confession must come before First Communion (Can. 914). Needed only if it was made at another parish.
documents.where: Parish where the child made First Reconciliation

documents.name: Religious education registration and attendance record
documents.detail: Enrollment in the program, and often proof of the prior year if the child transferred
documents.where: Parish faith formation office or previous program

documents.name: Parish registration
documents.detail: Many programs require the family to be registered

documents.name: Program fee
documents.detail: Some programs charge a registration or materials fee. Amounts vary, and assistance is usually available. Ask the parish.

documents.name: Photo or media release form
documents.detail: Many parishes restrict photography and use a single parish-arranged photographer

requirements: Attend parent meetings
Bring the child to Sunday Mass. Many programs ask families to attend regularly.

steps: Register at the parish and enroll the child in religious education (or the school program)
Submit the baptismal certificate
Complete First Reconciliation (usually in the same year)
Attend parent meetings, any retreat day, and the rehearsal
Ask about dress code, seating, and photography rules
Celebrate First Communion at the assigned Mass
classes: Usually a 2-year program (1st and 2nd grade) including First Reconciliation, often with a retreat day and a rehearsal. Children with disabilities are entitled to appropriate adaptation. Talk to the DRE.
dayOf: Arrive early for seating and line-up
Many parishes ask girls to wear a white dress (veil optional) and boys a dark suit or white shirt and tie. Follow your parish's dress code.
The child should observe the Eucharistic fast of one hour before Communion (water and medicine excepted) (Can. 919 §1)
Children receive Communion during Mass, on the tongue or in the hand
Photography is often limited during Mass. Posed photos usually happen afterward.
A certificate is typically given. The sacrament is recorded in the parish.

faq.q: My child has celiac disease. Can they receive?
faq.a: Yes. Ask the parish about low-gluten hosts approved for Mass, or about receiving from the chalice only. Arrange it before the day.

faq.q: Can my child receive First Communion at a family parish in another city?
faq.a: Often yes, with coordination. The preparation parish typically has to confirm the child is ready, and the receiving parish has to agree. Start early.

faq.q: Can non-Catholic family members receive Communion at the Mass?
faq.a: Ordinarily no. Non-Catholic guests are welcome to attend and pray, and many come forward with arms crossed to ask for a blessing, if the parish does that. The USCCB's guidelines for receiving Communion are often printed in missalettes.

title: Confirmation (young people)
summary: Confirmation completes baptismal grace with a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit, through anointing with chrism by the bishop or a priest he delegates. The USCCB permits Confirmation between the age of discretion and about age 16, and each diocese sets its own age. Many confirm in 7th–11th grade, and some 'restored order' dioceses confirm at about age 7, before First Communion. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Contact the parish youth ministry or DRE well before the confirmation year. Many dioceses require a 1–2 year program. The ceremony date depends on the bishop's schedule and is often in spring.
contact: The parish Director of Religious Education (DRE), youth minister, or Confirmation coordinator

documents.name: Baptismal certificate
documents.detail: Proves the candidate is baptized and tells the parish where to send the Confirmation notation. Many parishes require a recently issued copy if baptism was elsewhere.

documents.name: Proof of First Communion
documents.detail: Needed if First Communion was received at another parish

documents.name: Program registration form
documents.detail: Enrollment in the parish Confirmation program

documents.name: Sponsor certificate / letter of eligibility
documents.detail: From the sponsor's own parish, certifying they meet Can. 874 (via Can. 893). Not needed if the sponsor is registered at the confirming parish and the parish can verify it.

documents.name: Confirmation name form
documents.detail: Many US parishes have candidates choose a saint's name and write a short reflection on that saint. This is a custom, not a canonical requirement. Some candidates use their baptismal name, which the Church encourages as a link to baptism.

documents.name: Letter to the pastor or bishop
documents.detail: Some programs ask candidates to write a letter requesting Confirmation

documents.name: Service hours log
documents.detail: Many programs require Christian service hours. The number varies widely.
documents.where: Candidate; signed by the supervising organization

documents.name: Retreat permission and medical forms
documents.detail: For the required retreat, if any

documents.name: Program fee
documents.detail: Some programs charge for materials and retreats. Ask about the amount and whether help is available.

requirements: Chosen by the person being baptized, the parents, or (failing them) the pastor, and willing to take on the role (Can. 874 §1, 1°)
At least 16 years old, unless the diocesan bishop has set a different age or the pastor grants an exception for a just cause (Can. 874 §1, 2°)
A Catholic who has been confirmed and has received the Most Holy Eucharist (Can. 874 §1, 3°)
Leads a life of faith in keeping with the role (Can. 874 §1, 3°); in US practice this is usually read as attending Mass regularly and, if married, being in a marriage recognized by the Church
Not under a canonical penalty legitimately imposed or declared (Can. 874 §1, 4°)
Not the father or mother of the person being baptized (Can. 874 §1, 5°)
The same requirements as a baptismal godparent apply (Can. 893 §1)
It is desirable to choose one of the baptismal godparents (Can. 893 §2)
Only one sponsor is needed. Unlike baptism, Confirmation has no two-sponsor rule.
documents: Sponsor certificate / letter of eligibility from the sponsor's own parish

steps: Make sure the family is registered at the parish
Enroll in the Confirmation program and submit the baptismal certificate
Choose a sponsor and have them request a sponsor certificate from their parish
Complete classes, the retreat, and any service hours or interviews
Choose a Confirmation name if your parish follows that custom
Go to confession before the Confirmation Mass (strongly encouraged and usually scheduled)
Attend the rehearsal
Receive Confirmation from the bishop (or a delegated priest)
classes: Commonly 1–2 years of formation, often including a retreat, a pastor or DRE interview, and service. Requirements vary a great deal by diocese.
dayOf: Wear modest formal clothing. Some parishes use red or white robes.
The sponsor stands behind the candidate with a right hand on the candidate's shoulder
The candidate's chosen name is given to the bishop, often on a name card
The bishop anoints the forehead with chrism: 'N., be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.' The candidate answers 'Amen.' Bishop: 'Peace be with you.' Candidate: 'And with your spirit.'
A stipend/offering is customary for some parish expenses; ask the parish.
The Confirmation is recorded and a notation is sent to the parish of baptism

faq.q: Can a parent be the Confirmation sponsor?
faq.a: No. The sponsor must not be the candidate's father or mother (Can. 874 §1, 5°, applied by Can. 893 §1).

faq.q: Can my sponsor be a baptismal godparent?
faq.a: Yes, and the Church encourages it (Can. 893 §2).

faq.q: Can a non-Catholic be a Confirmation sponsor?
faq.a: No. The sponsor must be a confirmed Catholic who has received the Eucharist.

faq.q: What's 'restored order'?
faq.a: Some US dioceses confirm children at about age 7 and then give First Communion, restoring the historical order Baptism–Confirmation–Eucharist. Your diocese's policy decides which applies.

title: Confirmation for adults (baptized Catholics)
summary: For Catholics baptized in the Church who missed Confirmation as teenagers. Some also missed First Communion. Church law asks Catholics who are not yet confirmed to be confirmed before marriage if this can be done without grave inconvenience (Can. 1065 §1). Many adults seek it before a wedding or before becoming a godparent. Unbaptized adults, and baptized Christians from other churches, go through OCIA instead. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Contact the parish several months ahead. Many dioceses hold one adult Confirmation Mass a year, often around Pentecost, and parishes may confirm adults at the Easter Vigil or at a diocesan Mass.
contact: The parish office, adult faith formation director, or OCIA coordinator (many parishes prepare these adults alongside OCIA)

documents.name: Baptismal certificate with notations, recently issued
documents.detail: Proves Catholic baptism and shows whether Confirmation or marriage is already recorded

documents.name: Proof of First Communion
documents.detail: If received elsewhere. If you never made First Communion, tell the parish so it can be included in your preparation.

documents.name: Parish registration
documents.detail: Most parishes prepare their own registered parishioners

documents.name: Marriage information
documents.detail: If married, the parish asks whether the marriage is recognized by the Church. Generally a married adult must be in a valid marriage, or have it convalidated first, before Confirmation.
documents.where: Marriage certificate(s). Annulment decree if previously married.

documents.name: Sponsor certificate / letter of eligibility
documents.detail: From the sponsor's parish

documents.name: Letter of request or interview form
documents.detail: Some parishes ask adults to write a brief letter or meet the pastor

requirements: Chosen by the person being baptized, the parents, or (failing them) the pastor, and willing to take on the role (Can. 874 §1, 1°)
At least 16 years old, unless the diocesan bishop has set a different age or the pastor grants an exception for a just cause (Can. 874 §1, 2°)
A Catholic who has been confirmed and has received the Most Holy Eucharist (Can. 874 §1, 3°)
Leads a life of faith in keeping with the role (Can. 874 §1, 3°); in US practice this is usually read as attending Mass regularly and, if married, being in a marriage recognized by the Church
Not under a canonical penalty legitimately imposed or declared (Can. 874 §1, 4°)
Not the father or mother of the person being baptized (Can. 874 §1, 5°)
Same requirements as a baptismal godparent (Can. 893 §1). Must not be your parent, but may be your spouse if the spouse qualifies.
documents: Sponsor certificate / letter of eligibility from the sponsor's own parish

steps: Request your baptismal certificate with notations
Contact the parish and ask about adult Confirmation preparation and the next date
Resolve any marriage situation with the pastor first, if applicable
Choose a sponsor, who requests a sponsor certificate
Complete the preparation sessions
Make a confession before Confirmation
Be confirmed at the parish, Easter Vigil, or diocesan adult Confirmation Mass
classes: Adult sessions, often weekly for a few months, sometimes shared with OCIA. Content and length vary widely.
dayOf: Wear modest formal clothing
The sponsor places a right hand on your shoulder while you are anointed with chrism
A stipend/offering is customary at some parishes; ask the parish.
The parish records the Confirmation and notifies your parish of baptism

faq.q: Do I have to be confirmed to get married in the Church?
faq.a: Church law says unconfirmed Catholics should be confirmed before marriage if it can be done without grave inconvenience (Can. 1065 §1). Many US parishes arrange it during marriage prep, but it is not a condition for the marriage to be valid. Ask your parish.

faq.q: Do I have to be confirmed to be a godparent?
faq.a: Yes. A godparent must be a confirmed Catholic (Can. 874 §1, 3°).

faq.q: I was baptized Catholic but raised in another church. What path do I take?
faq.a: Usually adult Confirmation, often within the parish OCIA group for baptized Catholics. You do not make a 'reception into full communion'. Talk to the coordinator.

title: Marriage (two Catholics)
summary: Between two baptized persons, marriage is a sacrament: a lifelong, exclusive covenant open to children. Catholics marry validly when they exchange consent before a priest or deacon and two witnesses (canonical form, Can. 1108). Before the wedding, the Church must establish that nothing stands in the way of a valid and lawful marriage (Can. 1066). Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Contact the parish BEFORE booking a reception venue. Most US dioceses require at least 6 months' notice (some 8–12). Mass and church dates book up early. Allow extra time if either party was previously married.
contact: The parish office, usually the parish of the bride or groom. The priest or deacon who will witness the marriage handles the prenuptial investigation.

documents.name: Baptismal certificate with notations, issued within the last 6 months (each Catholic)
documents.detail: Shows baptism, Confirmation and freedom to marry (no prior marriage noted). Typical US practice is a certificate issued within 6 months of the request or the wedding.
documents.where: Each party's parish of baptism (see 'Sacramental records')

documents.name: Prenuptial questionnaire / premarital investigation
documents.detail: Each party answers questions, usually separately and often under oath, about freedom to marry, understanding of marriage, and intentions toward permanence, fidelity and children. This is how the parish meets Can. 1066–1067.
documents.where: Completed with the priest or deacon

documents.name: Affidavits of freedom to marry
documents.detail: Usually 1–2 per party, often from a parent or a long-time friend, attesting that you have never married. Some dioceses require these, especially when the baptismal certificate can't be recent.
documents.where: Witnesses who have known you most of your life; forms come from the parish

documents.name: Proof of Confirmation
documents.detail: If it isn't noted on the baptismal certificate. Unconfirmed Catholics are asked to be confirmed before marriage if possible without grave inconvenience (Can. 1065 §1).

documents.name: Marriage preparation completion certificate
documents.detail: Proof that you attended the required program (e.g. Pre-Cana, Engaged Encounter, a sponsor-couple program)

documents.name: Premarital inventory results
documents.detail: Many dioceses use an inventory such as FOCCUS or PREPARE/ENRICH, reviewed with the priest, deacon or a sponsor couple

documents.name: Natural Family Planning class certificate
documents.detail: Several US dioceses require an introductory NFP class. Others only recommend it.
documents.where: Diocesan NFP office or an approved provider

documents.name: Civil marriage license
documents.detail: Required by state law in every US state for the priest or deacon to officiate a marriage with civil effect. Rules and validity windows vary by state and county. Give it to the officiant before the ceremony.
documents.where: County clerk in the state where the wedding takes place

documents.name: Declaration of nullity (annulment) decree
documents.detail: Required for each prior marriage of either party, even a civil-only or non-Catholic marriage, unless the Church has already determined it was invalid for another reason
documents.where: The diocesan tribunal that handled the case

documents.name: Death certificate of a previous spouse
documents.detail: If either party is widowed

documents.name: Final civil divorce decree
documents.detail: For any prior marriage. Usually requested along with the annulment decree.
documents.where: The court that granted the divorce

documents.name: Delegation / letter of permission
documents.detail: If the wedding is at a parish other than either party's own, or with a visiting priest or deacon, or if paperwork is prepared in one diocese and the wedding is in another (the file is forwarded through the chanceries)

documents.name: Permission for special cases (Can. 1071)
documents.detail: The local ordinary's permission is needed in certain situations, for example: obligations from a prior union (such as to children of that union); one party has notoriously rejected the Catholic faith; a marriage that can't be recognized under civil law; or a minor marrying without parents' knowledge or reasonable consent
documents.where: Requested by the parish from the diocese

documents.name: Wedding planning form / liturgy worksheet
documents.detail: Your choice of readings, music, and ministers, from the Order of Celebrating Matrimony

people.role: Two witnesses (e.g. maid of honor and best man)
requirements: Two witnesses are required for validity (Can. 1108 §1)
Must be able to understand what they are witnessing. They do not have to be Catholic.
State law may set its own rules for license witnesses (age, number)
documents: Usually none for the Church. Their full names go in the register and on the civil license.

requirements: Must have the faculty to assist at marriages where the wedding takes place, or delegation from the pastor or local ordinary
documents: Delegation, if a visiting priest or deacon

steps: Call the parish before booking anything else and request a date
Meet the priest or deacon for an initial interview
Order baptismal certificates with notations, timed to be issued within the 6-month window
Complete the prenuptial questionnaire and gather affidavits of freedom to marry
If either party was married before, start the annulment process FIRST. You cannot set a firm wedding date until a decree is issued.
Complete the premarital inventory and marriage preparation program, plus NFP if required
Plan the liturgy: readings, music, whether Mass or a ceremony outside Mass
Obtain the civil marriage license within your state's validity window and give it to the officiant
Attend the rehearsal
After the wedding, the parish records the marriage and notifies each Catholic's parish of baptism
classes: Usually a marriage preparation program (Pre-Cana day, Engaged Encounter weekend, online program, or several sessions with a sponsor couple), a premarital inventory, and meetings with the priest or deacon. Some dioceses add an NFP class.
dayOf: Bring the civil marriage license if the officiant doesn't already have it
Witnesses, couple, and officiant sign the parish register and the civil license
The ceremony may be within Mass or outside Mass. Consent is exchanged before the priest or deacon and two witnesses.
A stipend/offering is customary for the church, and often separately for the priest or deacon, musicians and other staff; ask the parish.
Check parish rules on photography, flowers, aisle runners, and decorations

faq.q: Can we get married outdoors or at our venue?
faq.a: Ordinarily a marriage between Catholics takes place in a parish church (Can. 1118 §1). Another suitable place requires the local ordinary's or pastor's permission, and many US dioceses rarely grant it for venues. Ask early.

faq.q: Why do we need a baptismal certificate issued within 6 months?
faq.a: Any prior marriage would be noted on the baptismal record. A recent copy confirms that no marriage has been noted since. The 6-month window is common US practice, so check with your diocese.

faq.q: We're already living together. Can we still marry in the Church?
faq.a: Yes. Your priest or deacon will discuss it pastorally. It is not a canonical impediment.

faq.q: Is there a fee?
faq.a: Parishes commonly ask for an offering for use of the church and staff. Amounts vary. A stipend/offering is customary; ask the parish.

title: Marriage: Catholic & non-Catholic (mixed marriage / disparity of cult)
summary: A Catholic may marry a non-Catholic in the Church. The paperwork depends on whether the non-Catholic is baptized. A Catholic marrying a baptized non-Catholic Christian needs PERMISSION for a 'mixed marriage' (Can. 1124). The marriage is a sacrament. A Catholic marrying an unbaptized person needs a DISPENSATION from the impediment of disparity of cult (Can. 1086). Without it the marriage is invalid. Either way, a separate dispensation from canonical form is needed if the wedding will not take place before a Catholic priest or deacon (Can. 1127 §2). Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Contact the parish at least 6 months ahead (many dioceses require it), and earlier if a dispensation from form is needed or either party was married before. Permission and dispensation requests go through the diocese, which can take several weeks.
contact: The Catholic party's parish office. The priest or deacon prepares the file and submits requests to the diocese (chancery).

documents.name: Catholic party: baptismal certificate with notations, issued within the last 6 months
documents.detail: Proof of Catholic baptism and freedom to marry

documents.name: Non-Catholic party: proof of baptism
documents.detail: If the non-Catholic says they are baptized: a baptismal certificate from their church, or an affidavit from a parent or witness if no record exists. This decides whether permission (baptized) or dispensation (unbaptized) is needed. The parish confirms the baptism was valid (water + Trinitarian formula).
documents.where: The non-Catholic party's church of baptism

documents.name: Non-Catholic party: affidavit of non-baptism
documents.detail: If unbaptized: often a signed statement by the party, sometimes with a parent's statement

documents.name: Prenuptial questionnaire (both parties)
documents.detail: As for any Catholic marriage (Can. 1066–1067)

documents.name: Affidavits of freedom to marry (both parties)
documents.detail: Witness statements that each has never married. Especially important for the non-Catholic party, who has no Catholic notation record.
documents.where: Parents or long-time friends; forms from the parish

documents.name: Request for permission for a mixed marriage (Can. 1124)
documents.detail: Catholic + baptized non-Catholic. The pastor submits it to the local ordinary.

documents.name: Request for dispensation from disparity of cult (Can. 1086)
documents.detail: Catholic + unbaptized person. Needed for validity.

documents.name: Catholic party's declaration and promise (Can. 1125)
documents.detail: The Catholic declares they are prepared to remove dangers of falling away from the faith, and sincerely promises to do all in their power to have all children baptized and raised Catholic. The non-Catholic party does NOT promise anything, but must be informed of the Catholic's promise. In the US this is usually signed (oral or written per the norms of the conference, Can. 1126).

documents.name: Request for dispensation from canonical form (Can. 1127 §2)
documents.detail: Only if the wedding will be officiated by a non-Catholic minister or civil officiant, or held in a non-Catholic place of worship. The local ordinary grants it for a grave reason, and some public form is still required.

documents.name: Annulment decree / death certificate / divorce decree
documents.detail: For any prior marriage of EITHER party, including the non-Catholic's prior marriage, even one that was never in a Catholic church

documents.name: Marriage preparation and inventory certificates
documents.detail: As for any Catholic marriage. Some programs offer interchurch or interfaith sessions.

documents.name: Civil marriage license
documents.detail: Required by state law for the wedding to have civil effect

requirements: Two witnesses are required (Can. 1108)
They need not be Catholic

With a dispensation from form, a non-Catholic minister may officiate. Without one, a non-Catholic minister may take part (e.g. a reading, prayer or blessing), but the Catholic priest or deacon receives the consent.
documents: Dispensation from canonical form, if the minister will officiate

steps: Contact the Catholic party's parish early
Establish the non-Catholic party's baptismal status. This decides whether you need permission or a dispensation.
Gather certificates and affidavits for both parties
Resolve any prior marriages of either party through the tribunal first
The Catholic party makes the declaration and promise (Can. 1125). The non-Catholic party is informed of it.
The pastor submits the permission and/or dispensation request(s) to the diocese
If marrying in the other party's church or with their minister officiating, request a dispensation from canonical form
Complete marriage preparation
Plan the liturgy. A wedding between a Catholic and a non-Catholic usually takes place outside Mass. A Mass is sometimes possible for a Catholic and a baptized Christian. Ask your parish.
Obtain the civil license
classes: The same marriage preparation as for two Catholics, sometimes with sessions specific to interchurch or interfaith couples. Both parties are instructed on the ends and essential properties of marriage (Can. 1125, 3°).
dayOf: Bring the civil marriage license
The ceremony is often the Order of Celebrating Matrimony without Mass, which the Rite provides for. Disparity-of-cult weddings use the form for a Catholic and a catechumen or non-Christian.
Sign the parish register and the civil license
A stipend/offering is customary; ask the parish.
If a dispensation from form was granted for a wedding elsewhere, the marriage is still recorded in the Catholic party's parish. Make sure the officiant's certificate gets back to the Catholic parish.

faq.q: What's the difference between permission and a dispensation?
faq.a: Marrying a baptized non-Catholic Christian without permission (Can. 1124) is unlawful, but the marriage is still valid. Marrying an unbaptized person without a dispensation from disparity of cult (Can. 1086) is invalid. A dispensation from canonical form (Can. 1127) is a third, separate grant, needed only when the wedding won't take place before a Catholic priest or deacon.

faq.q: Does the non-Catholic have to convert or promise to raise the kids Catholic?
faq.a: No. Only the Catholic party makes the promise (Can. 1125). The non-Catholic is simply informed of it.

faq.q: Can we marry in my fiancé's church?
faq.a: Yes, with a dispensation from canonical form granted by the local ordinary (Can. 1127 §2). A Catholic priest or deacon may also attend.

faq.q: My fiancé is Eastern Orthodox. Is anything different?
faq.a: Yes. If an Orthodox priest officiates, the Catholic form is required only for lawfulness, not validity, but a sacred minister must be present for validity (Can. 1127 §1). Permission is still required. Talk to your pastor.

faq.q: Is a Catholic–unbaptized marriage a sacrament?
faq.a: No. It is a valid natural marriage, not a sacrament, because only marriage between two baptized persons is sacramental. If the unbaptized spouse is later baptized, the marriage becomes a sacrament.

title: Convalidation (having a civil marriage recognized by the Church)
summary: A Catholic who married outside the Church, before a judge or a non-Catholic minister without a dispensation from form, is not validly married in the eyes of the Church. Convalidation (often called 'having your marriage blessed') is a new exchange of consent in the canonical form. It makes the marriage valid, and sacramental if both are baptized. In some cases the bishop may instead grant a radical sanation, which validates the marriage without a new exchange of consent. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Contact the parish any time. If neither spouse was married before, the process often takes 1–6 months. Prior marriages must be resolved first, which can add a year or more.
contact: The parish office, usually with the pastor or a deacon

documents.name: Civil marriage certificate
documents.detail: Proof of the existing civil marriage, including its date and place
documents.where: County clerk or vital records where you married

documents.name: Baptismal certificate with notations, recently issued (each Catholic)
documents.detail: Often required to be issued within the last 6 months

documents.name: Non-Catholic spouse: proof of baptism or affidavit of non-baptism
documents.detail: Determines whether permission or a dispensation is needed (see the interfaith marriage entry)
documents.where: Spouse's church of baptism, or a parish form

documents.name: Prenuptial / pre-convalidation questionnaire (both spouses)
documents.detail: Establishes freedom to marry and an understanding of marriage

documents.name: Affidavits of freedom to marry
documents.detail: Witnesses attesting that neither spouse had another marriage before this one
documents.where: Parents or long-time friends; forms from the parish

documents.name: Annulment decree(s)
documents.detail: For ANY prior marriage of either spouse, including civil-only or non-Catholic marriages

documents.name: Death certificate of a prior spouse
documents.detail: If a spouse is widowed from an earlier marriage

documents.name: Permission or dispensation
documents.detail: Mixed marriage permission or disparity of cult dispensation, as for any interfaith marriage (Can. 1124, 1086)
documents.where: Requested by the parish from the diocese

documents.name: Proof of marriage preparation
documents.detail: Many dioceses require a shortened program suited to couples already married

requirements: Two witnesses are required, as for any Catholic wedding (Can. 1108)

steps: Talk to your pastor and explain the situation
Gather baptismal certificates and the civil marriage certificate
Resolve any prior marriages through the tribunal
Complete the questionnaire and affidavits
Complete any marriage enrichment or preparation the parish requires
Schedule the convalidation ceremony: a simple ceremony or a Mass, private or with guests
Exchange consent before a priest or deacon and two witnesses
The parish records the marriage. No new civil license is needed.
classes: Often a shortened or enrichment-style program for couples already civilly married, plus a meeting or two with the priest or deacon
dayOf: No new civil license is needed. You are already civilly married.
The ceremony can be simple and small, or a full celebration
Both spouses and two witnesses sign the parish register
A stipend/offering is customary; ask the parish.

faq.q: Is convalidation a 'renewal of vows'?
faq.a: No. A renewal of vows celebrates an existing valid marriage. Convalidation is a new act of consent that makes the marriage valid in the Church.

faq.q: Neither of us is Catholic. Do we need this?
faq.a: No. Non-Catholics are not bound by the Catholic form of marriage, and the Church presumes their marriage valid. If one of you becomes Catholic, nothing more is needed unless a prior marriage complicates things.

faq.q: Can we receive Communion before the convalidation?
faq.a: Talk to your pastor. A Catholic in a marriage the Church does not recognize is generally asked to resolve it before receiving Communion, and the pastor can guide you.

faq.q: What is a radical sanation?
faq.a: The competent authority validates a marriage without a new exchange of consent, typically when one spouse is unwilling or unable to take part in a ceremony but the consent persists (Can. 1161–1165). Ask your pastor whether it fits your case.

title: Declaration of Nullity (annulment)
summary: A declaration of nullity is a finding by a Church tribunal that a marriage, presumed valid, lacked something essential from the start, so a valid marriage bond never came into being. It is not a 'Catholic divorce', and it does not deny that the relationship existed. The Church treats any marriage as valid until proven otherwise, including those of non-Catholics. Anyone previously married (Catholic or not) generally needs one before marrying in the Church. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Start well before setting any wedding date. A formal case commonly takes about 12–18 months, but it varies widely by diocese and case. The shorter 'briefer process' and documentary cases can be much faster. Don't set a wedding date until you have a decree.
contact: Your parish priest, deacon, or a trained parish advocate first. They help prepare the petition for the diocesan tribunal.

documents.name: Final civil divorce decree
documents.detail: US tribunals generally require that the civil divorce be final before they accept a case
documents.where: The court that granted the divorce

documents.name: Civil marriage certificate
documents.detail: From the marriage being examined

documents.name: Church marriage certificate
documents.detail: If the marriage took place in a church
documents.where: The church or parish where you married

documents.name: Petitioner's baptismal certificate (if baptized)
documents.detail: Often a recently issued copy with notations

documents.name: Respondent's baptismal information
documents.detail: Baptismal certificate if obtainable, or at least religion and church of baptism. The parties' baptismal status affects which process applies.

documents.name: Petition (libellus) and the tribunal's questionnaire
documents.detail: A formal request, plus a detailed written history of the relationship: family backgrounds, courtship, wedding, married life and breakdown
documents.where: Tribunal forms, prepared with your advocate

documents.name: Former spouse's (respondent's) current contact information
documents.detail: The respondent must be notified and has the right to take part. Proceeding without an address requires showing that a diligent search was made.

documents.name: Witness list
documents.detail: Names and contact details of people who knew the couple before and during the marriage (often 2–5 witnesses). Family members can serve. Tell them to expect a questionnaire.

documents.name: Supporting records
documents.detail: Counseling or medical records, police reports, protective orders, etc., only if relevant and you are willing to release them
documents.where: Providers or courts, with your signed release

documents.name: Signed release / mandate for advocate
documents.detail: Authorizes your parish advocate or procurator to act for you

documents.name: Tribunal fee or offering
documents.detail: Pope Francis' 2015 reform (Mitis Iudex Dominus Iesus) urged that tribunal procedures be free of charge insofar as possible, and many US dioceses have since stopped charging. Others still request a fee or contribution, often with waivers. Costs vary, so ask your tribunal. Inability to pay should never prevent a case.

documents.name: Documentary case paperwork (lack of form)
documents.detail: If a Catholic married outside the Church without a dispensation, the case is usually a simple documentary process: Catholic baptismal certificate, civil marriage certificate, divorce decree, and proof that no convalidation took place
documents.where: Parish of baptism / county clerk / court

requirements: A priest, deacon, or trained lay advocate who helps you prepare the petition. Many dioceses train parish-level advocates.
People who knew you and/or your former spouse before and during the marriage
They answer a questionnaire or interview. Their testimony is confidential within the process.
Is notified and may participate, decline, or contest. The case can proceed without their cooperation.

steps: Make sure the civil divorce is final
Meet your priest, deacon, or parish advocate to discuss the marriage and which process applies (formal process, documentary case, or briefer process before the bishop)
Gather certificates and decrees
Write the petition and testimony using the tribunal's questionnaire
Provide witness names and the respondent's address
The tribunal reviews the petition, accepts the case, and notifies the respondent
The tribunal formulates the ground(s) to be examined (e.g. lack of due discretion, simulation, an impediment)
Evidence: witnesses are contacted, and sometimes expert evaluations are made
The Defender of the Bond argues for validity, and the parties may review the acts as the law allows
The judge(s) decide. Since the 2015 reform, an affirmative decision becomes final if no one appeals. A second confirming decision is no longer automatically required.
Receive the decree. Any restrictions (a 'vetitum' or monitum, such as counseling before remarriage) are noted.
The decision is noted in each Catholic party's baptismal record
classes: None. Some dioceses offer support groups for divorced Catholics.
dayOf: There is no ceremony. You may be asked to come in for an interview or give testimony in person or by video.
Keep your decree with your sacramental records. You will need it to marry in the Church.

faq.q: Does an annulment make my children illegitimate?
faq.a: No. Children born of a marriage entered in good faith are legitimate in Church law (Can. 1137), and an annulment has no civil effect on custody, support or property.

faq.q: Do I need an annulment if I'm divorced but not planning to remarry?
faq.a: No. Divorced Catholics who have not remarried remain in full communion and may receive the sacraments. An annulment is needed only to marry in the Church.

faq.q: My first marriage was between two non-Catholics. Do I still need one?
faq.a: Usually yes. The Church presumes non-Catholic marriages valid. Depending on the facts, other processes may apply, such as the Pauline privilege (Can. 1143) or a favor of the faith case. Ask your parish.

faq.q: What is the briefer process?
faq.a: Created by the 2015 reform. When both spouses petition or consent and the facts clearly show nullity, the case may go to the bishop for a quicker decision. The tribunal decides whether a case qualifies.

faq.q: How much does it cost?
faq.a: It varies. Many US dioceses no longer charge after the 2015 reform. Others ask a fee or contribution, often with waivers available. Ask your tribunal.

sources: Can. 1671–1691 (as revised by Mitis Iudex Dominus Iesus, 2015)

title: Anointing of the Sick (and 'last rites')
summary: Anointing of the Sick gives strength, peace and courage, forgives sins, and may restore health if God wills. It is for a Catholic who has reached the use of reason and is in danger because of serious illness or old age (Can. 1004 §1). It is not only for the dying, and it can be repeated (Can. 1004 §2). Only a priest can anoint (Can. 1003 §1). 'Last rites' usually means Confession, Anointing and Viaticum (Holy Communion for the dying), sometimes with the Apostolic Pardon. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Ask for it as soon as serious illness is diagnosed, before major surgery, when frailty sets in with age, or when a condition gets worse. Don't wait for the last hours.
contact: Non-emergency: the parish office. Emergency: the parish's emergency or after-hours line (the parish phone message often gives it), or in a hospital, the Catholic chaplain or the pastoral care / spiritual care office.

documents.name: No paperwork is required
documents.detail: Bring or provide the information below so the priest can find the person and prepare

documents.name: Person's full name and exact location
documents.detail: Hospital, room number, unit (ICU and the like), care facility, or home address, plus any entry codes or visiting restrictions

documents.name: Catholic status and condition
documents.detail: That the person is Catholic, whether they are conscious and able to talk, and whether they can swallow (for Communion)

documents.name: Hospital religious preference on file
documents.detail: List the patient's religion as Catholic at admission. Many hospitals use this to notify the Catholic chaplain.

documents.name: Contact person's phone number
documents.detail: So the priest can reach the family

requirements: Only a priest (or bishop) can anoint (Can. 1003 §1). A deacon or lay minister can pray with the sick and bring Communion, but cannot anoint.

steps: Non-emergency: call the parish office and ask for a visit, or ask about the parish's communal anointing Mass if offered

EMERGENCY: call the parish number and listen for the emergency option, or call your diocese's emergency line if it has one. In a hospital, ask the nurse to page the Catholic chaplain or spiritual care office.
If you can't reach your own parish, call any nearby Catholic parish. Priests respond to emergencies regardless of where the person is registered.
Give the person's name, location, and condition
If death seems near, say so clearly so the priest can bring Viaticum and give the Apostolic Pardon
While waiting, pray with the person (the Our Father, Hail Mary, or an act of contrition)
If the person has already died, still call. The priest can pray the prayers for the dead with the family. If it is uncertain whether death has occurred, the sacrament may be given (Can. 1005).
dayOf: The priest may hear the person's confession if they can make one. Give them privacy.
He lays hands on the person and anoints the forehead and hands with the Oil of the Sick
He may give Holy Communion (Viaticum, if death is near) and the Apostolic Pardon
Family may stay for the anointing and prayers
Have a quiet space, and if possible a table with a cloth, a crucifix and a candle (only if safe and permitted) at home
There is no fee. A stipend/offering is sometimes given; ask the parish.

faq.q: Can my non-Catholic husband receive Anointing?
faq.a: Ordinarily the sacrament is for Catholics. In grave necessity, certain other Christians who ask for it on their own and share Catholic faith in the sacrament may receive it under conditions in Can. 844. Ask the priest.

faq.q: Can it be given more than once?
faq.a: Yes. Again if the person recovers and falls seriously ill again, or if the condition gets worse in the same illness (Can. 1004 §2).

faq.q: Can I be anointed before surgery?
faq.a: Yes, if the surgery is serious, which many parishes interpret generously. Call the parish before the procedure.

faq.q: Can a person who is unconscious be anointed?
faq.a: Yes. If they would have asked for it while conscious, the sacrament is given (Can. 1006).

sources: Pastoral Care of the Sick: Rites of Anointing and Viaticum

title: Catholic Funerals (vigil, funeral Mass, committal)
summary: The Order of Christian Funerals has three main parts: the Vigil for the Deceased (often during the wake or visitation), the Funeral Liturgy (usually a Funeral Mass), and the Rite of Committal at the grave, tomb or columbarium. Deceased Catholics are entitled to Church funeral rites (Can. 1176 §1). The Church prefers burial of the body but permits cremation unless it is chosen for reasons contrary to Christian teaching (Can. 1176 §3). Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Call the funeral home first; it typically contacts the parish to set a date. A funeral Mass is usually scheduled within about a week of death, depending on the parish and cemetery calendars. Funeral Masses are not usually celebrated on Sundays of Advent, Lent and Easter, on solemnities of obligation, or during the Easter Triduum.
contact: The funeral home (usually contacts the parish for you), then the parish office or bereavement ministry coordinator. Also the cemetery, Catholic or otherwise.

documents.name: Death certificate
documents.detail: The funeral home usually files it and orders certified copies. Get several copies for banks, insurance, Social Security, etc.
documents.where: Funeral home, which files with the state or county vital records office

documents.name: Burial or cremation permit
documents.detail: Required by state law before burial or cremation. The funeral home obtains it.

documents.name: Funeral home contract
documents.detail: Choice of casket or urn, services and fees. Ask for the itemized General Price List, which the FTC Funeral Rule requires funeral homes to provide.

documents.name: Cemetery deed, plot, niche or columbarium information
documents.detail: Proof of ownership or right of interment, the section/lot/grave number, and cemetery contact details. Buy a space if you don't already own one.

documents.name: Deceased's basic information
documents.detail: Full name, dates of birth and death, parish, and (if known) the parish of baptism, for the funeral register

documents.name: Funeral planning worksheet
documents.detail: Your choices of readings, psalm, Gospel, music, readers, gift bearers, pallbearers, and any words of remembrance

documents.name: Military discharge papers (DD-214)
documents.detail: For military funeral honors, a VA-supplied headstone or marker, or burial in a national cemetery
documents.where: Family papers, or the National Archives (National Personnel Records Center)

documents.name: Pre-arranged funeral plans or insurance
documents.detail: If the deceased pre-planned or pre-paid

documents.name: Instructions about cremated remains
documents.detail: Where the ashes will be buried or entombed (cemetery, mausoleum, or columbarium)

documents.name: Obituary text
documents.detail: Often written with the funeral home's help. Include the time and place of the vigil, Mass and committal.

requirements: Typically one for the Old Testament (or, during the Easter season, the Acts of the Apostles) reading and one for the New Testament reading. The Gospel is read by the priest or deacon.
Family members or friends who can read clearly. Some parishes provide lectors.
Usually 6–8 people. Honorary pallbearers may also be named.
Many dioceses allow one family member or friend to speak briefly, often before the final commendation or at the vigil. Some limit it to the vigil or the reception. Ask your parish, and keep it short.

steps: At death: if a priest wasn't present, call the parish. The priest can still pray with the family.
Contact a funeral home. It transports the deceased, files the death certificate, and usually coordinates with the parish.
Contact or confirm the cemetery and burial or entombment arrangements
Meet the parish (priest, deacon or bereavement minister) to plan the liturgy and choose readings from the Order of Christian Funerals
Schedule the vigil (often at the funeral home or the church during visitation)
Arrange music with the parish music director
Prepare the obituary, and choose pallbearers and readers
Hold the Funeral Mass (or a funeral liturgy outside Mass), then the committal at the cemetery
Ask the parish to have Masses offered for the deceased in the months ahead (a stipend is customary)
dayOf: Vigil: Scripture, prayers, possibly a rosary and words of remembrance, usually during the wake

Funeral Mass: the casket is received at the church door and sprinkled with holy water, and the pall is placed on it. Then readings, homily, the Eucharist, and the final commendation and farewell (incense).
Committal: brief prayers at the graveside, mausoleum or columbarium
Bring the readings and the readers' names, and any item that symbolizes Christian life the parish allows (e.g. a Bible or crucifix placed on the casket)
Flags or other secular symbols are usually removed from the casket inside the church and replaced by the pall. Military honors happen at the committal.
A stipend/offering is customary for the parish, priest, musicians and servers; ask the parish. Funeral home and cemetery charges are separate.

faq.q: Can Catholics be cremated?
faq.a: Yes. Since 1963 the Church has permitted cremation unless it is chosen for reasons contrary to Christian faith. The Church still prefers burial of the body (Can. 1176 §3; Ad resurgendum cum Christo, 2016). The US Order of Christian Funerals prefers that the body be present for the Funeral Mass, with cremation afterward. A Funeral Mass with the cremated remains present is also permitted in US dioceses that allow it.

faq.q: What must be done with the ashes?
faq.a: According to Ad resurgendum cum Christo (Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, 2016), cremated remains must be laid to rest in a sacred place: a cemetery, a church, or an area set aside for that purpose by Church authority. They are NOT to be kept at home (except in grave and exceptional cases with the bishop's permission), divided among family members, scattered on land, at sea or in the air, or kept in jewelry or other mementos. A burial at sea in a proper, sealed, weighted container is generally treated differently from scattering. Ask the parish.

faq.q: Can the deceased have a Catholic funeral if they didn't practice?
faq.a: Usually yes. A Catholic funeral is denied only in narrow cases where it would cause public scandal (Can. 1184), such as notorious apostates or those who chose cremation for reasons contrary to the faith, and only if they gave no sign of repentance before death. When in doubt, the bishop decides. Talk to the priest.

faq.q: Can someone who died by suicide have a Catholic funeral?
faq.a: Yes. The Church commends them to God's mercy (CCC 2282–2283) and does not deny funerals on that ground.

faq.q: Can a non-Catholic spouse have a funeral in the Catholic Church?
faq.a: Possibly. Catechumens are treated like Catholics for funerals, and a baptized non-Catholic may be given a Catholic funeral at the local ordinary's prudent judgment if their own minister is unavailable and it isn't against their wishes (Can. 1183). Ask the pastor.

faq.q: How do we choose readings?
faq.a: The Order of Christian Funerals gives a list of options: Old Testament readings (e.g. Wisdom 3:1–9), psalms (e.g. Psalm 23), New Testament readings (e.g. Romans 6:3–9), and Gospels (e.g. John 14:1–6). The parish usually gives you a booklet with all of them.

sources: Order of Christian Funerals (incl. US Appendix on Cremation)

title: OCIA: becoming Catholic (Order of Christian Initiation of Adults)
summary: OCIA is how adults become Catholic. It was formerly called RCIA, and OCIA is the name used in the newer US translation of the rite. Unbaptized people (catechumens) receive Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion together. Baptized Christians from other churches (candidates) make a Profession of Faith and are received into full communion, with Confirmation and First Communion. Children of catechetical age (about 7 and up) follow an adapted version, often called OCIC or 'RCIC'. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Start any time: inquiry is often year-round. Unbaptized catechumens usually spend at least a full liturgical year in formation (US National Statutes) and receive the sacraments at the Easter Vigil. Baptized candidates may be received when they are ready, sometimes sooner and not necessarily at Easter. If you were married before, start the annulment process right away, because it is often the longest step.
contact: The parish OCIA coordinator, or the parish office, which will connect you

documents.name: Birth certificate
documents.detail: Used to record your legal name and date and place of birth
documents.where: State or county vital records office

documents.name: Baptismal certificate (baptized candidates)
documents.detail: Proof of a valid Christian baptism (water + Trinitarian formula) from your church. If no record exists, the parish may accept an affidavit from a witness. If validity is seriously doubtful, conditional baptism may be considered (Can. 869).

documents.name: Catholic baptismal certificate (baptized Catholics who were never catechized)
documents.detail: If you were baptized Catholic but never confirmed or never received First Communion, you complete initiation instead of being 'received'

documents.name: Marriage history and certificates
documents.detail: If you are married, or were ever married: civil and religious marriage certificates and any divorce decrees, for yourself and your spouse's prior marriages too. The Church must establish that your current marriage is valid, or can be, before you receive the sacraments.

documents.name: Declaration(s) of nullity
documents.detail: Required for each prior marriage of you or your current spouse before you can be received, unless another process applies (e.g. Pauline privilege). This is the most common reason for delay.

documents.name: OCIA registration / inquiry form
documents.detail: Personal information, religious background, and marital status

documents.name: Sponsor/godparent certificate
documents.detail: If your sponsor is not registered at your parish

documents.name: Letter or interview for the Rite of Election
documents.detail: Some parishes ask for a short written statement before the Rite of Election or Call to Continuing Conversion

documents.name: Saint's name (optional)
documents.detail: Some US parishes invite a Confirmation name. It is a custom, not a requirement.

documents.name: Children's version: child's birth and any baptismal certificates; parents' consent
documents.detail: Children of catechetical age need parental consent and involvement
documents.where: Parents / vital records / church of baptism

people.role: Sponsor (from the Rite of Acceptance) / godparent (from the Rite of Election)
requirements: Chosen by the person being baptized, the parents, or (failing them) the pastor, and willing to take on the role (Can. 874 §1, 1°)
At least 16 years old, unless the diocesan bishop has set a different age or the pastor grants an exception for a just cause (Can. 874 §1, 2°)
A Catholic who has been confirmed and has received the Most Holy Eucharist (Can. 874 §1, 3°)
Leads a life of faith in keeping with the role (Can. 874 §1, 3°); in US practice this is usually read as attending Mass regularly and, if married, being in a marriage recognized by the Church
Not under a canonical penalty legitimately imposed or declared (Can. 874 §1, 4°)
Not the father or mother of the person being baptized (Can. 874 §1, 5°)
The sponsor accompanies you during formation and attests to your readiness. The same person may continue as godparent, or a godparent may be chosen for the Rite of Election onward.
documents: Sponsor certificate / letter of eligibility from the sponsor's parish

requirements: Doesn't need to be Catholic, but must take part in reviewing the marriage history. Spouses are often welcome at sessions.
documents: Spouse's marriage history and baptismal information

steps: Contact the parish OCIA coordinator and attend inquiry sessions. Asking questions commits you to nothing.
Meet the coordinator or pastor for a personal interview: baptismal status and marriage history
Begin gathering documents. Start any annulment case immediately if needed.
Period of Evangelization and Precatechumenate (inquiry): learn about the faith and discern
