Unbaptized: the Rite of Acceptance into the Order of Catechumens begins the Catechumenate. Baptized candidates may have a parallel Rite of Welcoming.
Period of the Catechumenate: formation in Scripture, doctrine, prayer, and parish life. Catechumens are dismissed after the Liturgy of the Word to reflect on it.
First Sunday of Lent (or nearby): the Rite of Sending at the parish, then the Rite of Election (catechumens) and Call to Continuing Conversion (candidates) with the bishop, usually at the cathedral
Period of Purification and Enlightenment (Lent): the Scrutinies on the 3rd, 4th and 5th Sundays of Lent, and the Presentations of the Creed and the Lord's Prayer

Easter Vigil: catechumens receive Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion. Candidates make a Profession of Faith and receive Confirmation and First Communion (or are received at another time). Candidates make a sacramental confession beforehand.
Period of Mystagogy (Easter season through Pentecost): deeper reflection on the sacraments and life in the parish
classes: Weekly sessions are common for several months to a year or more. Unbaptized catechumens are expected to spend at least a year in the catechumenate (US National Statutes for the Catechumenate). Baptized, already-practicing Christians may need a shorter path. Children's OCIA (OCIC) runs alongside or within parish religious education, with parents involved.
dayOf: Rite of Acceptance: at a Sunday Mass, you are signed with the cross and welcomed
Rite of Election: usually at the cathedral with the bishop. Your name is enrolled in the Book of the Elect, and your godparent testifies.
Easter Vigil: begins after dark on Holy Saturday and lasts about 2–3 hours. Bring a change of clothes if baptism is by immersion. The parish usually provides white garments and candles.
Family and friends are welcome. Plan transportation and a celebration afterward.
There is usually no fee for OCIA. Some parishes ask for help with books or retreats; ask the parish.

faq.q: Is it RCIA or OCIA?
faq.a: The same process. The newer US translation calls the rite the 'Order of Christian Initiation of Adults', and many US dioceses have switched from 'RCIA' to 'OCIA'.

faq.q: I was baptized Lutheran (or Methodist, Baptist, etc.). Do I need to be baptized again?
faq.a: No. A valid Christian baptism is never repeated. You'll make a Profession of Faith and be received into full communion, with Confirmation and First Communion. Conditional baptism happens only if there's serious doubt that your baptism was valid (Can. 869).

faq.q: I'm divorced and remarried. Can I still join?
faq.a: You're welcome to inquire and attend. However, any prior marriage of you or your spouse must be resolved, usually through a declaration of nullity, before you can receive the sacraments. Start that process early.

faq.q: Do I have to wait until Easter?
faq.a: Unbaptized catechumens are normally baptized at the Easter Vigil. Baptized candidates may be received when the pastor judges they're ready, which may be another time of year.

faq.q: What about my 10-year-old who isn't baptized?
faq.a: Children who have reached the age of reason follow the children's adaptation (often called OCIC or RCIC). They receive Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion together, usually at the Easter Vigil.

sources: Order of Christian Initiation of Adults
USCCB National Statutes for the Catechumenate

title: Being a godparent or Confirmation sponsor
summary: A godparent (Baptism) or sponsor (Confirmation, OCIA) helps the person live the Christian life and fulfill the obligations of the sacrament (Can. 872). Church law sets minimum requirements (Can. 874). In the US you will almost always need a 'sponsor certificate' (also called a letter of eligibility or sponsor affidavit) from your own parish. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Request the sponsor certificate as soon as you're asked. Allow 1–4 weeks. Some parishes only issue certificates to people registered there for a period (often 3–6 months). Many baptizing parishes want it dated within the last 6 months.
contact: The parish office of the parish where YOU are registered (not the parish where the baptism or Confirmation will take place)

documents.name: Sponsor certificate / letter of eligibility
documents.detail: Signed by your pastor (or his delegate) with the parish seal, certifying that you are a practicing Catholic who meets Can. 874. Sent to you or to the baptizing or confirming parish.

documents.name: Sponsor request form
documents.detail: Many parishes ask you to fill out a form or sign a statement: confirmed, receive the Eucharist, attend Mass, and (if married) married in the Church

documents.name: Proof of your Confirmation
documents.detail: If your parish doesn't have your records, provide a baptismal certificate with notations or a confirmation certificate
documents.where: Your parish of baptism or confirmation

documents.name: Marriage information
documents.detail: If married, your parish may ask for proof that the marriage is recognized by the Church

documents.name: Proof of registration
documents.detail: Some parishes require that you have been registered and active for a minimum period

documents.name: Godparent class certificate
documents.detail: Some baptizing parishes require godparents to attend the baptism class
documents.where: The parish where you took the class

requirements: Chosen by the person being baptized, the parents, or (failing them) the pastor, and willing to take on the role (Can. 874 §1, 1°)
At least 16 years old, unless the diocesan bishop has set a different age or the pastor grants an exception for a just cause (Can. 874 §1, 2°)
A Catholic who has been confirmed and has received the Most Holy Eucharist (Can. 874 §1, 3°)
Leads a life of faith in keeping with the role (Can. 874 §1, 3°); in US practice this is usually read as attending Mass regularly and, if married, being in a marriage recognized by the Church
Not under a canonical penalty legitimately imposed or declared (Can. 874 §1, 4°)
Not the father or mother of the person being baptized (Can. 874 §1, 5°)
Only one godparent is required; if there are two, they must be one male and one female (Can. 873)
For Confirmation, the same requirements apply (Can. 893 §1), and choosing a baptismal godparent is encouraged (Can. 893 §2)
A baptized non-Catholic Christian may serve only as a Christian witness alongside a Catholic godparent, never as a godparent (Can. 874 §2). An unbaptized person cannot serve in either role.
documents: Sponsor certificate / letter of eligibility from your own parish

steps: Check that you meet the requirements, especially Confirmation, receiving the Eucharist, and (if married) a marriage recognized by the Church
Register at a parish if you haven't
Call your parish office and ask for a sponsor certificate for [name], whose Baptism or Confirmation is on [date] at [parish]
Fill out any request form and meet the pastor if asked
Send the certificate to the family or the baptizing or confirming parish by their deadline
Attend any required class or rehearsal
Stand with the person at the sacrament, and keep praying for them and supporting them afterward
classes: Sometimes the baptism class for godparents, or a sponsor session in Confirmation programs. Ask the parish where the sacrament will take place.
dayOf: Baptism: hold or stand near the child, renounce sin and profess faith with the parents, and often light the baptismal candle
Confirmation: stand behind the candidate with your right hand on their shoulder while the bishop anoints
Your name is recorded in the sacramental register

faq.q: Can I be a godparent if I'm not confirmed?
faq.a: No. A godparent must be a confirmed Catholic who has received the Eucharist (Can. 874 §1, 3°). If you were never confirmed, see adult Confirmation.

faq.q: Can a non-Catholic be a godparent?
faq.a: A baptized non-Catholic Christian may serve as a 'Christian witness' alongside a Catholic godparent, but not as the godparent (Can. 874 §2).

faq.q: I married outside the Church. Can I be a godparent?
faq.a: Usually not until the marriage is convalidated. Most US parishes read 'a life of faith in keeping with the function' (Can. 874 §1, 3°) to require a marriage recognized by the Church. Talk to your pastor.

faq.q: What age must a godparent be?
faq.a: At least 16 (Can. 874 §1, 2°), unless the diocesan bishop has set a different age or the pastor or minister grants an exception for a just cause.

faq.q: Can a parent be a godparent?
faq.a: No (Can. 874 §1, 5°). Grandparents, siblings, and other relatives may serve if they qualify.

faq.q: I don't belong to a parish. Can I still get a sponsor letter?
faq.a: Register at a parish, and talk honestly with the pastor. Some will issue a letter once they know you. Others require a period of active membership.

title: Holy Orders: discerning priesthood or the diaconate
summary: Holy Orders is the sacrament by which bishops, priests and deacons are ordained (only a baptized man can be validly ordained, Can. 1024). Diocesan priests serve a diocese, and religious priests belong to an order or congregation (e.g. Franciscans, Dominicans, Jesuits). Permanent deacons may be married. Discernment starts with a conversation, not paperwork. Requirements on this page combine universal Church law with common US practice. Dioceses and parishes vary, and your parish office has the final word.
timeline: Contact a vocation director at any time. Applications to seminary or diaconate formation usually follow months or more of discernment. Most US dioceses expect converts to have been Catholic for some time before applying (often a few years). Priestly formation commonly takes 6–8 years. Permanent diaconate formation commonly takes about 4–5 years after an aspirancy period.
contact: Your diocesan vocations director (priesthood) or the diocesan permanent diaconate office. For religious life, the vocation director of the community. Your pastor is a good first conversation.

documents.name: Baptismal certificate with notations, recently issued
documents.detail: Required for admission and before ordination

documents.name: Confirmation certificate
documents.detail: Confirmation is required before ordination (Can. 1033)

documents.name: Application packet
documents.detail: Autobiography, questionnaire, and references from your pastor and others

documents.name: Academic transcripts
documents.detail: High school and college, for seminary placement

documents.name: Psychological evaluation and medical exam
documents.detail: Standard in US seminary and diaconate admission

documents.name: Background check and safe-environment training
documents.detail: Required in US dioceses

documents.name: Parents' marriage and baptismal records
documents.detail: Some dioceses ask for these for the application file

documents.name: Permanent diaconate (married men): marriage certificate and wife's written consent
documents.detail: A married candidate needs his wife's consent (Can. 1031 §2). The marriage must be recognized by the Church.

documents.name: Annulment decree(s)
documents.detail: If either the candidate or his wife was previously married

requirements: A baptized Catholic man (Can. 1024), confirmed (Can. 1033)
Priesthood (Latin Church): generally unmarried and committed to celibacy. Minimum age for priestly ordination is 25 (Can. 1031 §1).
Permanent diaconate: a married man may be ordained no earlier than age 35, with his wife's consent (Can. 1031 §2). Dioceses often set their own maximum age at application.
Must be in good health, psychologically mature, and free of irregularities and impediments (Can. 1040–1049). The vocation office explains these.

steps: Pray, and talk with your pastor or a spiritual director
Contact the diocesan vocations director or the diaconate office (or a religious community's vocation director)
Attend discernment events, retreats, or a 'come and see' visit
Begin the formal application when the vocation director advises
Complete interviews, evaluations, and the documents listed here
If accepted: seminary or diaconate formation, with ongoing discernment throughout
classes: Seminary formation (often 6–8 years, depending on prior education) or diaconate formation (often 4–5 years after an aspirancy period). Religious communities have their own stages (postulancy, novitiate, vows).
dayOf: Ordination is celebrated by a bishop, usually at the cathedral. The ordinand lies prostrate during the Litany of Saints, then the bishop lays hands on him and says the Prayer of Ordination.

faq.q: I'm a recent convert. Can I apply?
faq.a: Usually after some years of active Catholic life. Many dioceses require at least 2–3 years. Ask the vocation director.

faq.q: Can married men become priests?
faq.a: In the Latin Church, generally no. Narrow exceptions exist (for example, some married former Protestant clergy received into the Church). Eastern Catholic Churches have their own discipline. Married men may become permanent deacons.

faq.q: What about women?
faq.a: Women may discern religious life as sisters or nuns, or consecrated virginity. Contact your diocesan vocations office or a religious community.

sources: USCCB National Directory for the Formation, Ministry, and Life of Permanent Deacons
